result: Schwann cells express Hdac4, 5, and 7 but not Hdac9 under normal conditions. In the dKO mice (lacking Hdac4 and Hdac5), Hdac7 expression is substantially induced (325.1 ± 48.1% at P60), while Hdac9 remains residual. This upregulation is specific to the dKO and can be detected early in development.
evaluation: Claims C1, C27-C30 are well-supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 1A and supplements) showing baseline expression patterns and compensatory Hdac7 upregulation in dKO mice. The specificity to dKO and early developmental detection are confirmed by supplementary data.

result: JUN mediates compensatory Hdac7 overexpression in dKO mice. JUN binds to the Hdac7 promoter (ChIP-qPCR), and a conserved JUN consensus binding motif was identified. Jun overexpression induces Hdac7 expression (~2-fold) specifically, while Jun removal does not affect basal Hdac expression. Hdac7 is not overexpressed in dKO mice lacking Jun (dKO;Jun_cKO).
evaluation: Claims C2, C31, C134-C145, C179-C181 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: ChIP-qPCR (Figure 8A), luciferase assays (Figure 8B showing 3.4-fold induction), RT-qPCR in Jun_OE and Jun_cKO mice (Figure 8D-F), and genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 8G). The mechanism is well-established.

result: Hdac7 upregulation compensates for the absence of Hdac4 and Hdac5, allowing myelination to proceed with some delay in dKO mice.
evaluation: Claims C3 and C34 are supported by morphological analysis showing delayed but eventual myelination in dKO mice (Figure 1 supplements), and by the observation that myelination proceeds normally after P8 despite initial delays.

result: Triple knockout (tKO) of Hdac4, 5, and 7 produces a much more pronounced delay in myelin development compared to dKO. Expression of negative regulators of myelination (including Jun) is notably increased from P2 to P21 in tKO mice. Despite the long delay, adult tKO nerves show almost normal myelination parameters.
evaluation: Claims C32, C33, C35 are well-supported by extensive morphological analysis (Figure 1B-J, Figure 2A-D) and gene expression data (Figure 1K-M) showing delayed myelination that eventually normalizes. The data demonstrate a gene-dose-dependent effect.

result: In tKO mice, Hdac9 (normally not expressed by Schwann cells) is de novo expressed to compensate for the absence of other class IIa HDACs. Hdac9 mRNA is increased 4.4-fold in adult tKO mice and is induced early in development (P2, P8). The Hdac9 promoter shows increased H3K9 acetylation in tKO nerves, and expression is further upregulated after nerve injury.
evaluation: Claims C4, C154-C161, C185 are strongly supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 9A-B), ChIP-qPCR showing increased H3K9Ac (Figure 9C), and RNA-seq data (Figure 9D-E). The de novo expression pattern is well-documented across developmental stages and injury conditions.

result: MEF2D regulates Hdac9 expression in tKO mice. Mef2d is upregulated in tKO nerves (RNA-seq, Western blot), is expressed by Schwann cells (SOX10+), and MEF2D binds to the Hdac9 promoter (ChIP-qPCR at 20 dpi). In the absence of class IIa HDACs, MEF2D is freed from repression and induces Hdac9 expression, as evidenced by increased H3K9Ac at the Hdac9 promoter.
evaluation: Claims C162, C164-C168, C189-C194 are well-supported by RNA-seq (Figure 9G), Western blot (Figure 9H-I), immunofluorescence (Figure 9J), and ChIP-qPCR (Figure 9K) data. The mechanism is consistent with known MEF2D-HDAC interactions from the literature.

result: In tKO mice, melanocytic lineage genes (Tyrp1, Mcam, Mitf, Ednrb) are misexpressed specifically in nonmyelin-forming Schwann cells of Remak bundles, and Remak bundle structure is disrupted with improper axon segregation. This suggests class IIa HDACs are necessary for proper Schwann cell precursor differentiation into Remak Schwann cells.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C36-C50, C203, C205-C207 are supported by RNA-seq (Figure 2F-I), RT-qPCR (Figure 3A-D), Western blot (Figure 3E-F), immunofluorescence (Figure 3G-K), and electron microscopy (Figure 2E) showing specific misexpression in Remak bundles and structural defects. The phenotype is specific to tKO.

result: Myelination proceeds after a long delay in tKO mice following nerve injury. At 10 dpi, no myelinated axons were found in tKO nerves (vs. 73±3.1% in controls). Myelination gradually recovers: 19.2±5.5% at 20 dpi, 60.3±6.1% at 30 dpi, with only slight delay at 60 dpi. Most unmyelinated axons are in 1:1 relationship with Schwann cells, suggesting delay in promyelinating to myelinating transition. The kinetics of remyelination is directly correlated with class IIa Hdac gene dose.
evaluation: Claims C7, C77-C90, C97 are extensively supported by morphological analysis (Figure 5D-N), Western blot (Figure 5O), and quantification of myelination parameters across multiple time points. The 1:1 relationship data (Figure 5I) supports the mechanistic interpretation.

result: In dKO mice, remyelination after nerve crush is notably delayed at 10 dpi (15.5±2.3% vs. 60.4±4.8% in controls) but normalizes by 30 dpi. The delay is due to intrinsic defects in activating the myelin transcriptional program (elevated Jun, Gdnf; decreased Krox-20, Periaxin, Mpz, Mbp), not altered repair phenotype activation or myelin clearance.
evaluation: Claims C58-C71 are well-supported by morphological analysis (Figure 4A-K), RT-qPCR (Figure 4L-M), Western blot (Figure 4N), and myelin clearance assays (Figure 4 supplement 3). The mechanistic interpretation is supported by gene expression data and normal repair marker expression.

result: tKO Schwann cells efficiently activate the repair phenotype after nerve injury, with some repair genes (Olig1, Shh) overexpressed at certain time points. Myelin clearance is accelerated in tKO nerves compared to controls, but without changes in autophagy markers or macrophage numbers.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76, C209-C211 are supported by RT-qPCR (Figure 5 supplement 2A-F), toluidine blue staining (Figure 5A), Western blot (Figure 5B-C), and immunofluorescence (Figure 5 supplement 2I). The lack of autophagy/macrophage changes (Figure 5 supplement 2G-I) is documented but the mechanism of accelerated clearance remains unexplained.

result: Electrophysiological studies show no differences in uninjured tKO nerves, but at 40 dpi after crush injury, tKO nerves show reduced responsiveness to electrical stimulation, decreased CAP amplitude for A-fibers (8, 10, 15V) and C-fibers (8, 10V), and decreased nerve conduction velocity (15V stimulation).
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by detailed electrophysiological recordings (Figure 6A-I) showing functional consequences of delayed remyelination. The data demonstrate that morphological delays translate to functional deficits.

result: ChIP-Seq analysis identified 3,932 HDAC4 binding peaks in differentiated Schwann cells, with 67.27% in proximal promoter regions. HDAC4 binds to promoters of multiple negative regulators of myelination (Jun, Gdnf, Runx2, Sox2, Id2, Hey2, Pou3f1, Mcam), supporting a role as a cAMP-regulated blocking hub for myelination repressors.
evaluation: Claims C117-C130, C221-C225 are well-supported by ChIP-Seq data (Figure 7A-H) with ChIP-qPCR validation. The breadth of targets supports the 'blocking hub' interpretation, though direct functional validation of all targets is not provided.

result: HDAC4 binds to promoters of highly expressed myelin genes (Mbp, Hmgcr). While seemingly contradictory, this is consistent with literature showing HDACs bound to active gene promoters, potentially functioning to reset chromatin modifications. Class IIa HDACs recruit class I HDACs via NCOR1/SMRT complexes and may have similar roles at active gene promoters.
evaluation: Claims C131-C133, C226-C232 are supported by ChIP-Seq data showing HDAC4 binding to Mbp and Hmgcr promoters. However, the functional interpretation is speculative, relying on analogy to class I HDACs in other systems (Wang et al., 2009). Direct functional validation of this proposed mechanism is lacking.

result: HDAC4 binds to the Hdac7 promoter in differentiated Schwann cells (ChIP-Seq and ChIP-qPCR), suggesting other class IIa HDACs maintain basal Hdac7 expression. In dKO mice lacking Hdac4/5, JUN can bind the derepressed Hdac7 promoter to stimulate compensatory expression.
evaluation: Claims C146-C148, C182-C184 are supported by ChIP-Seq (Figures 7B, 8H) and ChIP-qPCR (Figure 8I) data. The mechanistic model integrating HDAC4 repression and JUN activation is well-supported by the genetic and molecular data.

result: RNA-seq analysis of tKO nerves shows predominantly upregulated genes (654 up, 616 down in adult; increasing to 1895 up, 2450 down at 20 dpi after injury), suggesting class IIa HDACs function primarily as gene repressors. Negative regulators of myelination (Jun, Runx2, Gdnf, Ngfr, Sox2, Pou3f1) are upregulated, while myelin genes (Krox-20, Drp2, Prx, Mpz, Mbp, Mag, Pmp22, Plp1) and lipid biosynthesis genes (Hmgcs, Lss, Dhcr24, Elovl1, Pmp2, Scd2, Fads1, Cers2, Ugt8a) are downregulated.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41, C98-C116, C196-C197, C212-C214 are extensively supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2F-I, Figure 5 supplements 4-5) showing consistent patterns across developmental and injury time points. The gene expression changes are consistent with the myelination phenotypes observed.

result: Hdac4 removal (cKO4) has a small impact on remyelination with decreased myelinated axons at 10 dpi, increased unmyelinated axons >1.5μm, and subtle changes in myelin gene expression. Myelin clearance is normal. The impact is compensated after 10 dpi.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by morphological analysis (Figure 4 supplement 1F-K), RT-qPCR (Figure 4 supplement 1L-N), and myelin clearance assays (Figure 4 supplement 1O). The mild phenotype supports the redundancy hypothesis.

result: Hdac5 removal (KO5) shows no differences in remyelination morphology, myelin protein gene expression, or myelin clearance compared to wild-type littermates.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by morphological analysis and gene expression data (Figure 4 supplement 2). The lack of phenotype supports the redundancy model.

result: Hdac5 partially compensates for Hdac4 loss in vivo. Only removal of both Hdac4 and Hdac5 leads to obvious myelination delay. By P8, myelination in dKO mice proceeds at the same pace as wild-type, suggesting an additional compensatory mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are supported by citations to previous work (Gomis-Coloma et al., 2018) and morphological data in Figure 1 supplement 5 showing delayed but normalized myelination by P8 in dKO mice.

result: Background on Schwann cell myelination: Immature Schwann cells downregulate Jun (negative regulator) and upregulate Krox-20/Yy1 (positive regulators) during development. Jun is reexpressed after injury for repair phenotype, then downregulated to allow remyelination. cAMP/Gpr126 signaling promotes myelination via HDAC4 nuclear shuttling, which recruits NcoR1/HDAC3 to repress Jun and promote Krox-20 expression.
evaluation: Claims C10-C22 are well-established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to prior literature and the authors' previous work. These provide the conceptual framework for the current study.

result: Discussion of genetic redundancy: Gene redundancies are evolutionarily conserved and can buffer against gene expression noise. Class IIa HDAC redundancy in Schwann cells ensures myelination program activation. Responsive backup circuits mediated by JUN and MEF2D coordinate compensatory mechanisms to repress negative regulators of myelination, ensuring Schwann cell differentiation and myelin formation during development and after injury.
evaluation: Claims C169-C177, C233-C236 synthesize the experimental findings with established concepts of genetic redundancy. The conclusions are well-supported by the extensive experimental data presented, though the evolutionary/noise-buffering interpretation is somewhat speculative.

result: Discussion of melanocytic gene misexpression: Tyrp1 (most upregulated gene in tKO) is involved in melanin synthesis, but tyrosinase is not expressed and Tyrp1 mRNA is not translated to protein. Tyrp1 mRNA may have non-coding functions (e.g., sequestering miR-16). Melanocytes can derive from Schwann cell precursors, and axonal signals normally repress melanocytic lineage in SCPs.
evaluation: Claims C198-C202, C204 are supported by RNA-seq, Western blot (Figure 2 supplement 1D), and citations to literature. The functional interpretation of untranslated Tyrp1 mRNA is speculative but grounded in published mechanisms.

result: Discussion of remyelination mechanisms: Class IIa HDAC removal delays remyelination. Many genes upregulated in injured tKO nerves are expressed by nonmyelinating/repair Schwann cells (Jun, Runx2, Gdnf, Ngfr, Sox2, Pou3f1). Class IIa HDACs work as corepressors of transcription factors like MEF2 and RUNX2. Pou3f1 overexpression delays myelination and may contribute to tKO phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C208, C215-C220 integrate experimental findings with literature on HDAC function and Pou3f1. The interpretation is well-supported by RNA-seq data and citations, though the specific contribution of Pou3f1 to the phenotype is not directly tested.

result: Summary of compensation mechanisms: Hdac4/5 removal upregulates Hdac7 (JUN-mediated), allowing delayed myelination. Hdac9 is de novo expressed in response to class IIa HDAC gene dose drop. Hdac9 is induced in dKO;Jun_cKO mice (cannot overexpress Hdac7). Other class IIa HDACs can theoretically block Hdac9 expression in control nerves.
evaluation: Claims C178, C186-C188, C191 summarize key findings that are well-supported by the experimental data. The theoretical inference about HDAC repression of Hdac9 (C191) is reasonable based on known HDAC-MEF2 interactions.

result: Hdac9 expression patterns: Adult tKO nerves have morphologically normal myelin but 1270 differentially expressed genes. Hdac9 is normally not expressed or at extremely low levels in C57BL/6 mouse sciatic nerves and cultured rat Schwann cells. Hdac9 is among the most robustly upregulated genes in tKO nerves (4.4-fold increase, p<0.0001), with smaller increases in cKO7 (2.4-fold) and cKO4 (1.3-fold).
evaluation: Claims C195, C150-C153, C185 are supported by RNA-seq (Figure 2H), RT-qPCR (Figure 9A), and citations to previous work and databases (SNAT). The gene-dose-dependent pattern of Hdac9 induction is well-documented.
